packet.prompt:
Read only the supplied manuscript images. Do not search for the text, open a
catalogue or edition, or consult an earlier transcription. Do not identify the
work or author. If prior context has already revealed a proposed identification
or reading, stop and report that exposure instead of calling this a blind reading.

Begin with a brief image-only layout survey. Note orientation, columns, running
titles, rubrics, enlarged initials, underlined text, and interlinear or marginal
glosses when visible. Distinguish observations from tentative interpretations
such as main text with commentary. Do not infer author, work, date, or provenance.
A tight crop may not show the layout; say so rather than guessing.

Use those features to choose a few useful spans: headings or question openings,
then connecting prose, transitions or citation chains. Keep quoted lemmata and
commentary separate. Read enough surrounding prose to make a later source match
checkable; a full transcription is not required. State which areas you selected
and which remain unread. Suggest a wider view or an adjacent crop if needed.

Transcribe those spans, preserving physical lines. Label each line with its
image filename and a line number counted from the top of that image. Keep columns
and marginal additions separate. Note overlapping crops rather than treating
repeated lines as additional text.

Retain abbreviation marks when possible. Put proposed expansions in parentheses,
uncertain readings before a question mark, and unreadable text in [illegible].
Describe visible deletions and additions explicitly. Do not supply missing words
from what would make grammatical or philosophical sense. Leave uncertainty visible.

Return the reading as UTF-8 plain text. Include limitations (cropped lines, damage,
uncertain column order) in that same response. This is an unverified image reading.

text:
PACKET-13 - unverified image reading

Exposure statement: Nothing in my context revealed a proposed identification or an
earlier reading of this fragment. Beyond the rules, I made enlarged, contrast-
enhanced crops of the packet tiles in a private scratch folder. No other source
was opened.

=====================================================================
LAYOUT SURVEY
=====================================================================
A narrow vertical strip (about 5 x 21 cm on the scale) cut from a leaf, probably
a binding strip. Two faces:
- Face 1: overview image-001 (the left half of the frame is masked grey);
  tiles image-002 (upper) and image-003 (lower), which overlap by ~7 lines
  (image-002 lines 21-26 = image-003 lines 1-6). Pencil note "Stams, STA,
  Frg. 37r(?)" at the bottom (image-003).
- Face 2: overview image-004; tiles image-005 (upper) and image-006 (lower),
  overlapping by ~6 lines (image-005 lines 26-31 = image-006 lines 1-6). Pencil
  note "Stams, STA, Frg. 37v" (image-006).

Face 1 shows the LEFT part of a single text column: line beginnings with a
ruled left boundary, line ends cut off at the right edge of the strip (about 3-5
words per line survive). Face 2 shows the RIGHT part of a column: line ends
with a ruled right boundary (a strong vertical ruled line, image-006), line
beginnings cut off at the left, then a blank outer margin.

Script: a fast late-medieval Gothic cursive (bastard/current cursive), dark
brown ink, long descenders on f and long s, looped ascenders. Rubrication:
red paraph/capital strokes before many words, and red underlining of words or
phrases (these underlined words look like headwords or keyed terms; e.g.
"Villa", "Villicus", "villicatio(?)" in face 1). Red "stroke" marks also through
initial capitals within lines. A large red smudge/blot at the left edge of
face 1 (image-002 l.24 / image-003 l.5). Several red dots/double strokes ("..")
used as punctuation (e.g. image-002 l.7, l.20).

Face 2 margin: a red marginal note to the right of the column (image-006 at
about l.13): "ad sol(?)ne" / "ad s(er)mone(?)" - uncertain, red ink, followed by
two strokes. Also on face 2, over and to the right of the text there is faded
brown text in a larger textualis book hand (image-005, image-006 right side and
interlinear areas at the top) - this looks like OFFSET (transfer) from another
leaf that was pressed against this one, not writing on this leaf. It may be
mirror-reversed; I did not attempt to read it.

Tentative interpretation (not an identification): the content in face 1 looks
lexical/definitional - a word ("villa") is treated with its derivatives and
declension ("nomina", "declinatur(?)", "villicus", "villicatio(?)",
"villula(?)") - with red-underlined key terms. Face 2 has more discursive
phrases ("ad memoriam", "talenta", "passiones", "ad aquilonem(?)",
"multis modis"). This is an observation of vocabulary, not a claim about the work.

=====================================================================
TRANSCRIPTION
=====================================================================
Conventions: (x) = expansion; word? = uncertain; [...] = cut off at the strip
edge; [illegible]. <u>..</u> = underlined in red. [¶] = red paraph/capital
stroke. Line numbers from the top of each image.

=====================================================================
SELECTED AREAS / UNREAD
=====================================================================
Selected: the full surviving width of each line on both faces, with the most
confidence in face 1 lines 9-24 (the "villa/villicus/custos" passage) and face 2
lines 13-23 of image-005. Many words remain [illegible] or uncertain because the
cursive is fast and often only 1-2 words survive per line before the cut. The
offset textualis on face 2 was not read.

=====================================================================
LIMITATIONS
=====================================================================
- Only a fragment of each line survives (strip width): face 1 lacks line ends,
  face 2 lacks line beginnings. Whether face 1 and face 2 lines align as the
  recto/verso of the same column is not checked.
- Red underlining sometimes makes the underlined word harder to read (the red
  line crosses the lower part of the letters).
- Overlaps between upper and lower tiles were not counted twice.
- A brighter, higher-resolution image or UV would help with the faded first
  lines of face 2 (image-005 l.1-4), which are also overlaid by the offset text.
